summary: Specifies the base architecture for systems that implement IPsec, the family of protocols that secure IP traffic. It explains the security services offered, how security associations and policies work, and how the pieces fit together. It was a proposed standard, replaced by RFC 4301.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2401 explains how IPsec applies security services to IP traffic using policies, security associations, and keys. It was later updated by RFC 3168 and replaced by RFC 4301.

subtitle: The IPsec architecture for security policies, associations and packet processing.

tldr.problem: IP does not by itself provide all the security services that hosts and gateways may need. Systems need a shared architecture for selecting protections, managing keys, and applying them to traffic.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2401 defines Security Associations for AH or ESP, policy and association databases, traffic selectors, key management, and rules for processing inbound and outbound packets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2401 obsoletes RFC 1825, was updated by RFC 3168, and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4301. RFC 4301 is the later IPsec architecture.

today: RFC 2401 was obsoleted by RFC 4301 and was updated by RFC 3168. The unit metadata also records that RFC 2401 obsoletes RFC 1825.

sections.title: What IPsec Protects
sections.content:
IPsec provides security services at the IP layer for IPv4 and IPv6 traffic. These services include access control, integrity, data-origin authentication, replay protection, confidentiality, and limited traffic-flow confidentiality. Because protection is applied at the IP layer, higher-layer protocols can use it.

The architecture describes two traffic protocols: the Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). It also covers security associations, key management, and the algorithms used for authentication and encryption. The RFC states that IPsec is one part of system security, not an overall security architecture for the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec can protect IP packets from unauthorized access, changes, replay, or disclosure. The protection it provides depends on the selected protocol and configuration.

sections.title: Security Associations and Modes
sections.content:
A Security Association (SA) is a one-way connection that applies AH or ESP security services to traffic. An SA uses one protocol, not both. Two SAs are needed for ordinary two-way communication. An SA is identified by a Security Parameter Index, the IP destination address, and the security protocol.

Transport mode protects upper-layer protocols; tunnel mode protects a tunneled IP packet. When an SA endpoint is a security gateway acting as a gateway, the SA must use tunnel mode. AH can protect selected IP-header fields as well as upper-layer data. ESP can provide encryption and may also provide authentication and replay protection.
sections.plainLanguage: An SA protects traffic in one direction, so two are needed for two-way communication. Transport mode protects upper-layer traffic, while tunnel mode carries a protected IP packet inside another IP packet.

sections.title: Policy and Association Databases
sections.content:
The Security Policy Database (SPD) defines what happens to inbound and outbound traffic. A matching policy can discard a packet, let it bypass IPsec, or require IPsec processing. Policies use selectors such as source and destination addresses, transport protocol, ports, and names to identify traffic.

The Security Association Database (SAD) stores parameters for active SAs, including protocol, keys, algorithms, mode, sequence information, and lifetime. An inbound SA is looked up using the destination address, IPsec protocol, and SPI. SPD entries are ordered so that the first matching policy is selected consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The SPD decides which traffic to discard, pass without IPsec, or protect. The SAD stores the parameters for the security associations that protect traffic.

sections.title: Processing IP Packets
sections.content:
For outbound traffic, the system checks the packet against the SPD and finds the required SA or SA bundle. If a suitable SA does not exist, key management can establish one; otherwise, the packet is processed according to policy. For inbound traffic, the system uses the packet's IPsec protocol and SPI to find an SA, applies its protection, and checks the result against inbound policy.

An SA bundle applies multiple SAs in a defined order when one SA cannot provide the required combination of services. The RFC also defines required combinations for hosts and gateways and discusses handling of ICMP messages and path MTU information. The details of implementation can vary, but the externally visible behavior must match the architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: For outgoing traffic, the system finds the policy and applies the required protection. For incoming traffic, it finds the matching association, checks the packet, and verifies that the policy was followed.

sections.title: Managing Associations and Keys
sections.content:
IPsec requires support for both manual and automated security-association and key management. Manual configuration can be used for small or static arrangements, while automated management is intended to support larger deployments and association maintenance. The RFC identifies IKE as the default automated key-management approach and permits other automated methods.

Key management establishes the SAs and keying material needed by AH or ESP. The RFC does not define how a host automatically discovers or verifies its security gateway; it says that this information must be configured by an administrator.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec systems can configure keys manually or use an automated key-management protocol. The RFC identifies IKE as the default automated method but allows others.
